title: The Dal Khalsa and the council
hookLine: Sikh bands unite, meeting at Amritsar and deciding together before the Guru

lines: THE GROUP CHAT THAT NEVER DECIDES.
cards: A simple plan can take three days in a group chat. Everyone has an opinion, two people aren't speaking, and in the end nothing happens.
Now make the group many independent bands of riders, each with its own leader, its own pride, its own old quarrels. And the stakes aren't dinner plans. They're survival.
The Sikhs of the 1740s found a way to make that group decide, and stick to it. It happened twice a year, in Amritsar. Today: gurmata.

teach.h: GUR + MATA — A DECISION BEFORE THE GURU.
teach.b: Gurmata joins two words: gur, the Guru, and mata, a resolution, a considered decision. A gurmata is a decision made in the presence of the Guru, and so binding on everyone.
Even in the hunted years, the scattered Sikh bands tried to gather at Amritsar at Vaisakhi in spring and Diwali in autumn. The whole assembly was called the Sarbat Khalsa, the entire Khalsa.
They met before the Akal Takht, with the Guru Granth Sahib present. Leaders who might be rivals the rest of the year sat down together, and old quarrels were supposed to be left at the door.

Matters were discussed openly, and when the assembly agreed, it was sealed with Ardas, the prayer. From then on it was a gurmata: not one leader's plan but the Guru's decision, and every band was bound by it.
A turning point came at Vaisakhi, 1748, two years after the small holocaust.

teach.h: THE SARBAT KHALSA MEETS AT AMRITSAR.
teach.b: The Sarbat Khalsa resolved to bring the many bands together into one army, the Dal Khalsa, the army of the Khalsa, under a single commander, Jassa Singh Ahluwalia.
What gave the decision its weight wasn't the loudest voice or the biggest band. It was the presence of the Guru, and the agreement of the whole.
The Sikh Rehat Maryada, the Sikh code of conduct, still describes how a gurmata is made. There's a small lesson in it for any family or team.
A decision made together, in front of what everyone respects, holds better than one forced through. And the thing everyone bows to can be bigger than anyone in the room.

how: Sikh assemblies still pass gurmatas, resolutions made in the presence of the Guru Granth Sahib and sealed with Ardas; the Sarbat Khalsa, a gathering of the whole community at the Akal Takht, is the traditional forum.

o: a decision made together before the Guru
a single leader's order to his own band
the Guru's teaching, written in scripture

s: a gurmata was the plan of the strongest leader
it was the agreement of the gathered Khalsa in the Guru's presence.
the Sarbat Khalsa gathered at Vaisakhi and Diwali
in spring and autumn, before the Akal Takht in Amritsar.

games.q: Vaisakhi, 1748. many proud Sikh bands, each with its own leader, meet at Amritsar. what do they decide?
o: to split up for good, each on its own.
to join as one army, the Dal Khalsa, under one commander.
to choose the biggest band's leader as king.
games.why: the Sarbat Khalsa's gurmata united the bands into the Dal Khalsa, under Jassa Singh Ahluwalia.

practice: Think of a decision coming up that affects other people: what to cook, where to go, how to split a job, a family plan. Notice whether you meant to decide it yourself, or let it drift.
Then picture asking the others, listening properly, and choosing together, with something you all care about in the middle of the table.

wordCard.voice: Gurmata. A decision made by the gathered Khalsa in the presence of the Guru, and binding on all. Gur, the Guru, and mata, a resolution.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: gurmata, from gur (the Guru) and mata (a resolution).

carryVoice: Your line: decide together. Many voices, one decision. Day two hundred eighty-nine, done.
